message.content:
Two research tasks, both need primary-source grounding. Return a cited markdown digest with two sections.

SECTION A — World models for robotics/control (2023–2026): I made a first-principles judgment that a robotics-control project with an analytic simulator (PyBullet) does NOT need learned neural world models (Dreamer/Genie/JEPA-class), because the sim IS the world model and learned sims lie worse. I need to check this against the literature — try to REFUTE me, don't just confirm.
1. Current state: DreamerV3 (Hafner et al.), Genie/Genie-2 (DeepMind), JEPA/V-JEPA (LeCun/Meta), TD-MPC2, world models for robotic manipulation (e.g., UniSim, DayDreamer — Dreamer on real robots).
2. The strongest case FOR learned world models in a project like mine: DayDreamer showed sample-efficient learning on REAL robots; residual/hybrid models (analytic sim + learned correction); world models used to model CONTACT specifically — is there evidence learned models handle contact-rich manipulation better than analytic rigid-body sims? (Contact dynamics is notoriously bad in analytic sims — my project hit a rigid-contact numerical artifact.)
3. The case against / limits: hallucinated dynamics, compounding rollout error, data requirements, evaluation difficulty of learned sims.
4. Verdict material: for a small classical-control prototyping project on known rigid-body dynamics, what does the field actually recommend?

SECTION B — Long-horizon agent capability measurement + scalable oversight:
1. METR's "Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks" (2025) — the 50%-task-completion time horizon metric, the doubling trend (~7 months), what it says about how long agents can run without human intervention, and any 2025–2026 updates.
2. METR / others on agent reliability at long horizons: success rate vs task length falloff; the gap between 50% and 99% reliability horizons (this gap matters — my case needed ~10h of agent work).
3. Scalable oversight literature relevant to "human catches what the agent misses": recursive reward modeling, weak-to-strong generalization (Burns et al., OpenAI 2023), critique models (Saunders et al. 2022, "Self-critiquing models for assisting human evaluators"), any results on HUMANS+AI critique catching more than either alone.
4. Anything on the human-oversight bottleneck in agentic workflows — how oversight cost scales with agent throughput.

For each item: source + date, specific finding/number, 1-line takeaway. ~12-16 sources total across both sections. Primary sources. Return markdown.

Goal: build the STRONGEST possible case that learned world models / learned dynamics ARE useful even for a small robotics project that already has an analytic simulator (PyBullet) — i.e., try to REFUTE the claim "the analytic sim IS the world model, learned sims add nothing for known rigid-body dynamics."

Find primary sources (arXiv, CoRL/RSS/ICRA/ICLR papers, official project pages) on:

"Augmenting physical simulators with stochastic neural networks" (2018), Heiden et al. NeuralSim (ICRA 2021, differentiable sim + neural augmentation), "grounded action transformation" or sim2real residual dynamics learning.

Look for: papers critiquing rigid contact models in sims (e.g., Parmar/Halm/Posa "Fundamental challenges in deep learning of stiff contact dynamics" or Posa lab work showing BOTH analytic and learned models struggle with stiff contact), ContactNets (Pfrommer, Halm, Posa 2020), work showing learned contact models outperforming penalty/LCP solvers on real data (e.g., Bauza & Rodriguez on pushing stochasticity, planar pushing "More than a million ways to be pushed" showing real contact is stochastic and analytic models are biased).
4. Real2sim / system identification with learned components for quadrotors specifically — e.g., Neural-Fly (Caltech, Science Robotics 2022, learned residual aerodynamics for agile flight in wind), NeuroBEM (RPG Zurich, quadrotor dynamics hybrid model).

For EACH: title, authors, venue+date, URL, the specific quantitative finding (e.g., TossingBot 85% throw accuracy, Neural-Fly error reduction), and a 1-line statement of how it argues FOR learned components. Also note honestly where the evidence supports learned RESIDUALS on real data rather than replacing an analytic sim in pure simulation. WebFetch primary sources to confirm numbers. <result># Learned world models vs. "the analytic sim IS the world model" — evidence dossier

The strongest version of the counter-case, built from primary sources. Organized by the four threads, with confirmed numbers, then an honest scoping note.

## 1. Learning without any simulator — DayDreamer

**DayDreamer: World Models for Physical Robot Learning** — Wu, Escontrela, Hafner, Goldberg, Abbeel. CoRL 2022. [arXiv:2206.14176](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.14176) · [project page](https://danijar.com/project/daydreamer/) · [code](https://github.com/danijar/daydreamer)

- Quantitative: A1 quadruped learns to roll off its back, stand, and walk **from scratch in 1 hour, directly on hardware, no simulator, no resets**; adapts to pushes within **10 minutes**. Also: UR5/XArm pick-and-place from pixels + sparse reward approaching human-teleop rates, and Sphero navigation from pixels — **same hyperparameters across all four robots**.
- Argument FOR: the learned world model (Dreamer's latent dynamics) is sample-efficient enough that the analytic sim is *optional* — the world model is fit to the only ground truth that matters (the real robot), so it captures everything the analytic sim gets wrong by construction. The authors' stated motivation is exactly the refutation you want: simulators "fail to capture the complexity of the real world [and are] prone to simulator inaccuracies."
- Caveat: this replaces the sim for *policy training on real hardware*; it says little about a project whose entire universe is PyBullet.

## 2. Residual / hybrid physics — analytic model + learned correction

**TossingBot: Learning to Throw Arbitrary Objects with Residual Physics** — Zeng, Song, Lee, Rodriguez, Funkhouser. RSS 2019 / T-RO 2020 (Best Systems Paper, King-Sun Fu Memorial Award). [arXiv:1903.11239](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.11239) · [project page](https://tossingbot.cs.princeton.edu/)

- Quantitative (confirmed from paper tables): real-robot throwing accuracy **Residual-physics 84.7% seen / 82.3% unseen** vs **Physics-only (analytic ballistics) 61.3% / 58.5%** vs Regression-PoP 54.2% / 52.0%. Human baseline 80.1%±10.8. 600+ grasps/hour. The residual exists precisely because ballistics is biased: aerodynamic drag on light objects and off-COM grasps make the "correct" analytic release velocity systematically wrong.
- Argument FOR: this is the *closest possible comparable* to drone-catch — ballistic throwing to a target. The analytic model supplies structure and generalization (physics-only beats pure learning by a wide margin), but a **small learned residual on the release-velocity parameter buys +23 percentage points over analytics alone**. Physics as prior + learning as corrector beats either pure strategy.

**Augmenting Physical Simulators with Stochastic Neural Networks: Case Study of Planar Pushing and Bouncing** — Ajay, Wu, Fazeli, Bauza, Kaelbling, Tenenbaum, Rodriguez. IROS 2018. [PDF](https://jiajunwu.com/papers/physplus_iros.pdf) · [project hub](http://sain.csail.mit.edu/)

- Finding: an analytic rigid-body simulator augmented with a neural net that learns the *residual as a stochastic distribution* outperforms both the analytic sim alone and pure nets on real pushing and bouncing data; the hybrid also models the *uncertainty* of outcomes, which deterministic analytic sims cannot represent at all.
- Argument FOR: real contact outcomes are distributions, not points; the analytic sim can only ever emit the mode.

**NeuralSim: Augmenting Differentiable Simulators with Neural Networks** — Heiden, Millard, Coumans (PyBullet's author), Sheng, Sukhatme. ICRA 2021. [arXiv:2011.04217](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.04217) · [project page](https://uscresl.org/publication/neuralsim-augmenting-differentiable-simulators-with-neural-networks/)

- Finding: neural augmentations inserted *inside* a differentiable rigid-body engine learn effects the analytic model omits (frictional contact details from real data, viscous friction), need less data and generalize better than fully learned models; plus a 10× speedup replacing a QP in a quadruped MPC gait controller, validated on hardware. Notable: co-authored by Erwin Coumans — **the builder of PyBullet arguing analytic engines "can only predict systems for which they have been designed."**
- Argument FOR: even the people who write analytic simulators treat them as a prior to be corrected, not the world model.

**Grounded Action Transformation for Robot Learning in Simulation** — Hanna & Stone. AAAI 2017. [paper page](https://www.cs.utexas.edu/~pstone/Papers/bib2html/b2hd-AAAI17-Hanna.html) · [AAAI](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/11044)

- Finding: learn a small forward model of *real* NAO dynamics, use it to warp simulator actions so sim trajectories match reality; yielded a bipedal walk **43.27% faster than the state-of-the-art hand-coded walk** — a policy that raw-sim training could not transfer.
- Argument FOR: the fix for sim inaccuracy was not more careful analytic modeling but a learned correction layer.

## 3. Contact dynamics — where rigid-body solvers are weakest

**More than a Million Ways to Be Pushed** — Yu, Bauza, Fazeli, Rodriguez. IROS 2016 (dataset) and **A Probabilistic Data-Driven Model for Planar Pushing** — Bauza & Rodriguez, ICRA 2017. [arXiv:1704.03033](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017arXiv170403033B/abstract) · [MIT DSpace](https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/119860) · follow-up [Omnipush dataset](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.00618)

- Finding: high-fidelity repeated pushing experiments show real frictional contact is **stochastic and analytic models are biased**; a heteroscedastic-GP learned model **outperforms the analytic pushing model after fewer than 100 real samples** and saturates under 1000. Companion work ([Friction Variability in Planar Pushing Data](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.10089)) shows friction is anisotropic and drifts — not a constant μ as every analytic solver (PyBullet included) assumes.
- Argument FOR: on *real measured contact*, the analytic model is not just noisy — it is wrong on average, and trivially small amounts of data beat it.

**ContactNets: Learning Discontinuous Contact Dynamics with Smooth, Implicit Representations** — Pfrommer\*, Halm\*, Posa. CoRL 2020. [arXiv:2009.11193](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.11193) · [PMLR](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v155/pfrommer21a.html) · [code](https://github.com/DAIRLab/contact-nets)

- Finding: learns inter-body signed distance + contact Jacobians implicitly (complementarity/max-dissipation loss) and predicts realistic impact, non-penetration, and stiction of a real tossed cube from **60 seconds of real data**, where naive end-to-end nets fail.
- Argument FOR: the *structure* of contact can be kept while the *parameters and geometry* are learned from reality — a middle path that beats both hand-specified solver constants and unstructured learning.

**Fundamental Challenges in Deep Learning for Stiff Contact Dynamics** — Parmar, Halm, Posa. IROS 2021. [arXiv:2103.15406](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.15406) · [author note](https://matthalm.net/updates/contact-learning-bias)

- Finding: contact stiffness alone degrades naive deep-learning of dynamics (chaos, under-fitting, poor generalization) — **and** the authors explicitly flag that soft-contact *simulated* test environments "do not accurately reflect the stiffness of rigid robotic hardware."
- Argument FOR (double-edged, use honestly): this cuts against *naive* learned models, but its headline implication is that the compliant contact settings analytic sims use to stay numerically stable misrepresent real hardware — i.e., the analytic sim is not ground truth for contact either. It motivates structured learned contact (ContactNets), not solver faith.

## 4. Quadrotor-specific learned dynamics

**NeuroBEM: Hybrid Aerodynamic Quadrotor Model** — Bauersfeld, Kaufmann, Foehn, Sun, Scaramuzza (RPG Zurich). RSS 2021. [arXiv:2106.08015](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.08015)

- Quantitative: blade-element-momentum analytic model + learned residual, trained on 1.8 M datapoints / 96 agile flights (up to 65 km/h). **~50% force/torque RMSE reduction** (to 0.335 N / 0.012 N·m) vs prior models; closed-loop position RMSE **~0.8 m → <0.3 m**. Key ablation: the hybrid **outperforms both** pure BEM and pure learned dynamics — the learned-only model fails to generalize to unseen flight regimes.
- Argument FOR: for quadrotors specifically, first-principles rigid-body + rotor theory demonstrably leaves half the force error on the table; the missing half is aerodynamic interaction effects no analytic model captures.

**Neural-Fly Enables Rapid Learning for Agile Flight in Strong Winds** — O'Connell, Shi, Shi, Azizzadenesheli, Anandkumar, Yue, Chung (Caltech). Science Robotics, May 2022. [DOI](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/scirobotics.abm6597) · [arXiv:2205.06908](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.06908) · [code+data](https://github.com/aerorobotics/neural-fly)

- Quantitative (confirmed from Table 1): learned residual aerodynamic force (DAIML pretraining on **12 minutes** of flight data + online linear adaptation) inside a nominal-dynamics controller. Mean tracking error in 12.1 m/s wind: **8.7 cm vs 21.6 cm** for the nonlinear baseline (2.5×); overall **66% better than nonlinear baseline, 42% better than L1, 35% better than INDI**.
- Argument FOR: the winning architecture is exactly "analytic model where it's right, learned term where it's wrong" — and the learned term is what enables agile flight the analytic-only controller cannot deliver.

---

## The synthesized argument (and the honest boundary)

**Strongest form of the case.** (1) The claim "known rigid-body dynamics" is false at the two places drone-catch physically lives: *aerodynamics* (NeuroBEM: 50% of force error is unmodeled; Neural-Fly: 2.5× tracking gap; TossingBot: drag biases ballistics enough to cost 23 points of throw accuracy) and *contact* (Bauza/Yu: real contact is stochastic and analytic models are biased, beaten by <100 samples; Parmar/Halm/Posa: the compliant-contact settings sims need for stability don't reflect rigid hardware). (2) The dominant published architecture is not "learned sim replaces analytic sim" but **analytic prior + learned residual**, which beats both parents in every head-to-head found (TossingBot, NeuroBEM, Ajay et al., NeuralSim) — so the dichotomy in the claim is a false one. (3) Where no sim exists or the sim is wrong, learned world models are now sample-efficient enough to be trained on the real system directly (DayDreamer: 1 hour) — the analytic sim is a convenience, not a necessity.

**Honest scoping caveats.**
- Nearly all the quantitative wins are **learned residuals fit to real-world data**, correcting a real analytic-model/reality gap. None of these papers shows a learned model beating PyBullet *at predicting PyBullet* — inside a pure simulation project, the analytic sim is tautologically the ground truth, and a learned copy of it can only add error (plus speed, which is the actual argument for learned sims in pure-sim settings: NeuralSim's 10× MPC speedup, or imagination rollouts à la Dreamer being far cheaper than stepping the engine).
- Parmar/Halm/Posa is partly evidence *against* naive learned dynamics: stiffness breaks vanilla deep nets. The refutation must route through *structured* learning (ContactNets) or residuals, not end-to-end nets.
- DayDreamer's result is about policy learning sample-efficiency, not model fidelity; its "simulators are inaccurate" motivation applies to sim2real ambitions, which this project (CLAUDE.md §7, "Sim2real gap") explicitly defers.
- So the defensible thesis for this project is narrow but real: **the moment drone-catch cares about anything PyBullet models wrongly or not at all — propwash on the catch line (parking-lot #11 notes PyBullet can't test the wash claim), Re-dependent ball drag, stochastic contact at the fingertips, real-hardware transfer — the literature's answer is a learned residual on top of the analytic model, with strong precedent in this exact task family (TossingBot) and this exact vehicle class (NeuroBEM, Neural-Fly).**

## The case against learned world models where an analytic simulator exists — primary sources

### 1. Compounding model error / rollout divergence in MBRL

**When to Trust Your Model: Model-Based Policy Optimization (MBPO)** — Janner, Fu, Zhang, Levine. NeurIPS 2019. https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.08253
- Confirmed from full PDF: monotonic-improvement bound has a term `k/(1−γ)·ε_m` — the return gap grows **linearly in rollout length k times model error ε_m**. Verbatim: "the analysis relies on running full rollouts through the model, allowing model errors to compound" and "This result agrees with our theoretical analysis which prescribes short model-based rollouts to mitigate compounding modeling errors."
- In practice MBPO uses branched rollouts of **k = 1** (Dyna-style) up to a schedule of **k = 1→15** on Hopper; "single-step rollouts provide a baseline that is difficult to beat." Prior compounding-error work "evaluate[s] on truncated versions of benchmarks" because extended rollouts diverge.
- **Takeaway:** even the flagship MBRL success only trusts its learned model for ~1–15 steps; an analytic sim is trusted for the full horizon.

**Objective Mismatch in Model-based Reinforcement Learning** — Lambert, Amos, Yadan, Calandra. L4DC 2020 (PMLR 120:761–770). https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04523
- Confirmed: "the likelihood of one-step ahead predictions is not always correlated with control performance" — training a dynamics model on prediction loss optimizes the wrong objective for control.
- **Takeaway:** a learned model that scores well on its own training metric can still be the wrong model for the task — a failure mode analytic sims don't have.

### 2. Hallucinated dynamics / physics violations in video world models

**Do Generative Video Models Understand Physical Principles? (Physics-IQ)** — Motamed, Culp, Swersky, Jaini, Geirhos (Google DeepMind). arXiv Jan 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09038
- Confirmed scores (100% = physical-variance upper bound): **best model VideoPoet-multiframe 29.5%; Sora 10.0%**; Lumiere 23.0, Runway Gen 3 22.8, SVD 14.8, Pika 13.0. "Physical understanding is severely limited, and unrelated to visual realism" — Sora is the *most visually realistic* (55.6% MLLM detection, near chance) yet near-worst on physics; no significant realism↔physics correlation.
- **Takeaway:** looking right and being right are uncorrelated; the most convincing rollouts can be the most physically wrong.

**VideoPhy** — Bansal et al. arXiv Jun 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.03520
- Confirmed: best model (CogVideoX-5B) follows both caption and physical laws in only **39.6%** of instances across solid-solid/solid-fluid/fluid-fluid interactions.
- **Takeaway:** >60% physics failure rate for the best T2V model on basic material interactions.

**WorldModelBench** — Li et al. arXiv Feb 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.20694
- Confirmed from full text: 14 frontier models, 67K human labels, 7 domains incl. robotics/driving. Best model (KLING): only **61% of videos finish the specified task; 12% violate mass conservation; 11% show object interpenetration**. Across all models: impenetrability violated ~23% of the time, mass conservation ~18%.
- **Takeaway:** even the best "world model" video generators violate conservation laws in ~1-in-8 rollouts — laws an analytic sim satisfies by construction.

### 3. Data requirements (vs. zero for an analytic sim)

- **DreamerV3** — Hafner et al., Nature 2025 / https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04104. Learns from scratch, but the celebrated Minecraft-diamond result took **~30M env steps for the first diamond (~17 days of in-game play), <100M steps to do so reliably** (figures from the [project page](https://danijar.com/project/dreamerv3/) / Nature coverage, not the arXiv abstract — flagged accordingly).
- **TD-MPC2** — Hansen, Su, Wang. ICLR 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.16828. Multi-task agent (317M params, 80 tasks) trained on **545M transitions** harvested from replay buffers of **240 single-task agents** (confirmed via [tdmpc2.com/dataset](https://www.tdmpc2.com/dataset)).
- **V-JEPA 2** — Assran, Bardes et al. (Meta). arXiv Jun 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09985. Confirmed: pretrained on **>1 million hours** of internet video + ~62 hours of robot data for the action-conditioned variant.
- **Genie** — Bruce et al. (Google DeepMind). ICML 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15391. Confirmed from full text: **55M clips ≈ 244,000 hours raw, filtered to 30,000 hours** for training, 11B params. (The commonly cited "200k hours" slightly undercounts the raw set; only ~30k hours were actually used.)
- **Takeaway:** the learned route costs 10⁴–10⁶ hours of data plus training compute to approximate what `pybullet.setGravity(0,0,-9.81)` gives you exactly, for free, for known rigid-body dynamics.

### 4. Evaluation difficulty: no ground truth for a learned sim

**How Far is Video Generation from World Model: A Physical Law Perspective** — Kang et al. (ByteDance). arXiv Nov 2024, ICML 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.02385
- Confirmed: on a controlled 2D physics testbed, diffusion video models achieve near-perfect **in-distribution** prediction but **fail out-of-distribution**; generalization is **"case-based"** — mimicking the nearest training example, with attribute priority **color > size > velocity > shape** (i.e., the model keys on color before dynamics). Conclusion: **"scaling alone is insufficient"** to uncover physical laws.
- **Takeaway:** learned dynamics interpolate memorized cases rather than encode laws — precisely the regime (novel states) where you need a simulator most.
- WorldModelBench (above) doubles as the eval-difficulty citation: judging physics adherence required **67K human labels** plus a fine-tuned 2B judge model — validating a learned sim is itself an unsolved, label-hungry problem. (I did not find a dedicated "UniSim critique" paper; flagged as not confirmed.)

### 5. Survey statements: when analytic sims remain preferable

**World Models for Robotic Manipulation: A Survey** — Wang et al. arXiv May 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00113
- Confirmed quotes: "pixel-space objectives allocate modeling capacity to lighting, texture, background clutter… while manipulation success often depends on contacts, object permanence, force closure… Rollouts can therefore look coherent while violating the physical constraints"; "A policy trained in a learned environment may discover behaviors that exploit model artifacts rather than transferable manipulation skills."
- **A Survey: Learning Embodied Intelligence from Physical Simulators and World Models** — Long et al. arXiv Jul 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00917 — frames physics simulators as providing "controlled, high-fidelity environments… safe and efficient" and positions the two as **complementary**, not world-models-replace-sims.
- **Flag:** no survey I found states outright "use an analytic sim when dynamics are known" — the field's framing is "complementary." The strongest explicit support for that position is the combination of §1 (short-horizon-only trust), §2 (conservation-law violations), and §4 (case-based memorization + no ground-truth eval).

# METR Time-Horizon Research — Verified from Primary Sources

## 1. "Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks" (Kwa, West, et al.)

**Source:** [METR blog, Mar 19, 2025](https://metr.org/blog/2025-03-19-measuring-ai-ability-to-complete-long-tasks/) + [arXiv 2503.14499](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499) (submitted Mar 18, 2025; v3 Feb 25, 2026; lead authors Thomas Kwa, Ben West, Joel Becker, Amy Deng, Katharyn Garcia + 20 co-authors)

- **Metric definition (blog, verbatim):** model ability characterized by "the length (for humans) of tasks that the model can successfully complete with x% probability"; abstract: "the time humans typically take to complete tasks that AI models can complete with 50% success rate."
- **Doubling time (blog, verbatim):** task length completable "autonomously with 50% reliability has been doubling approximately every 7 months for the last 6 years." Abstract (v3): "doubling approximately every seven months since 2019, though the trend may have accelerated in 2024."
- **Claude 3.7 Sonnet:** blog: "time horizon of approximately one hour"; v1 abstract: "around 50 minutes"; TH1.1 re-estimate (2026): **60.4 min** [33.0–104.2]. ⚠️ The oft-cited "59 min" point estimate is presumably in a paper table — I confirmed "~50 min"/"~1 hour"/60.4 min, not the literal 59 figure.
- **Extrapolation:** paper (v3): ">1 month (167 work hours) between mid-2028 and mid-2031"; abstract: "within 5 years… tasks that currently take humans a month" (≈2030). Blog sensitivity analysis: 2024–25 data alone pulls this ~2.5 years earlier.
- *Takeaway: 50%-horizon has doubled ~every 7 months since 2019; frontier (Mar 2025) ≈ 1 hour; month-long tasks ≈ 2028–2031.*

## 2. 50% vs 80% gap; higher-reliability horizons

- **v1 (§4.2.1, verbatim):** for 80% reliability, "horizons are roughly 5x shorter." **v3 wording:** "models' 80% time horizons are 4-6x shorter"; 80%-horizon doubling time (204 days) ≈ 50%-horizon's (207 days).
- **99%:** the paper itself discusses only 50% and 80% — **no 99% figure in the paper** (flagged). The explicit statement is in METR's [Clarifying limitations of time horizon note, Jan 22, 2026](https://metr.org/notes/2026-01-22-time-horizon-limitations/): "Time horizons at 99%+ reliability levels cannot be fit at all without much larger and higher-quality benchmarks," and "a 50% time horizon of X hours does not mean we can delegate tasks under X hours to AIs."
- *Takeaway: demanding 80% instead of 50% reliability cuts the horizon ~5x; 99% horizons are unmeasurable with current suites — reliability, not raw capability, is the binding constraint for delegation.*

## 3. 2025–2026 updates (newer models, faster doubling)

**GPT-5 eval report** ([metr.org/evaluations/gpt-5-report](https://metr.org/evaluations/gpt-5-report/), Aug 7, 2025): 50%-horizon **2h17m** [65 min–4h25m]; 80%-horizon **~25 min** [8–65 min]; "a somewhat better fit for the faster trend observed from January 2024 through February 2025."

**Time Horizon 1.1** ([blog, Jan 29, 2026](https://metr.org/blog/2026-1-29-time-horizon-1-1/)): suite 170→228 tasks, 8h+ tasks 14→31, migrated to Inspect. Doubling times: post-2023 **131 days** (vs 165 under TH1); post-2024 **89 days**; full-period hybrid 196 days. ⚠️ I could not confirm a literal "4-month" METR quote — the confirmed acceleration figures are 131/89 days (TH1.1) and the paper's "may have accelerated in 2024."

**Current numbers** ([metr.org/time-horizons](https://metr.org/time-horizons/), last updated May 8, 2026; raw `benchmark_results_1_1.yaml`, units = minutes, verified against the "~1 hr" Claude 3.7 anchor). 50%-horizon [CI] / 80%-horizon:

| Model (release) | 50% | 80% |
|---|---|---|
| Claude 3.7 Sonnet (2025-02) | 60 min | 12 min |
| o3 (2025-04) | 2h00m | 30 min |
| Claude Opus 4 / 4.1 (2025-05/08) | ~1h40m | 20–24 min |
| GPT-5 (2025-08) | 3h23m [1.9–6.8h] | 38 min |
| Gemini 3 Pro (2025-11) | 3h44m | 54 min |
| GPT-5.1 Codex Max (2025-11) | 3h44m | 51 min |
| Claude Opus 4.5 (2025-11) | **4h53m** [2.7–10.4h] | 49 min |
| GPT-5.2 (2025-12) | 5h52m | 66 min |
| GPT-5.3 Codex / GPT-5.4 (2026-02/03) | ~5h45m | ~54 min |
| Gemini 3.1 Pro (2026-02) | 6h24m | 90 min |
| Claude Opus 4.6 (2026-02) | ~12h [5.3–60h] | 70 min |
| Claude Mythos Preview Early (2026-04) | ~17.4h [8.5–55h] | 3h06m |

METR caveat on the page: "Measurements above 16 hrs are unreliable with our current task suite." Gemini 2.5 Pro is not in the v1.1 dataset. Note GPT-5's 3h23m is the TH1.1 re-estimate; the Aug 2025 report's 2h17m was under TH1.0 — same model, different suite.

**Caveats** (limitations note, Jan 22, 2026): "Time horizon is not the length of time AIs can work independently" but "the amount of serial human labor they can replace with a 50% success rate"; domain variation "40–100x lower for visual computer use"; error bars ~2x each way ("I really have no idea whether Claude's 'true' time horizon is 3.5h or 6.5h"); benchmark tasks are low-context, well-defined, non-messy vs real work. Paper: "performance is much lower on less structured, 'messier' tasks," though the *trend* is similar across messiness subsets; "external validity concerns" are "the majority of our uncertainty."

- *Takeaway: as of mid-2026 frontier 50%-horizons are ~5–12+ hours (80%-horizons ~1–3 h), doubling every ~3–4.5 months post-2023 — but METR itself flags the >16 h measurements and real-world transfer as shaky.*

## 4. Success-vs-length falloff models

- **METR logistic fit** (arXiv 2503.14499 v3): `p_success = σ((log h_agent − log t_task)·β_agent)` — sigmoid in log task length; R² ≈ 0.80 regressing success on log human time-to-complete.
- **HCAST** ([arXiv 2503.17354](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17354), Rein et al., Mar 21, 2025): 189 tasks, 1 min–8+ h, 563 human baselines (1500+ h); "current agents succeed 70–80% of the time on tasks that take humans less than one hour, and less than 20% of the time on tasks that take humans more than 4 hours."
- **Sinha et al.** ([arXiv 2509.09677](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09677), "The Illusion of Diminishing Returns: Measuring Long Horizon Execution in LLMs," Sep 11, 2025, ICLR 2026; Sinha, Arun, Goel, Staab, Geiping): "marginal gains in single-step accuracy can compound into exponential improvements in the length of tasks"; identifies **self-conditioning** — models get *more* error-prone when their own prior mistakes are in context, and scaling alone doesn't fix it; "thinking mitigates self-conditioning, and also enables execution of much longer tasks in a single turn."
- *Takeaway: success falls off smoothly (logistic in log-length); the mechanism is compounding per-step error amplified by self-conditioning on past mistakes.*

## 5. Autonomy duration and oversight cadence

- **METR limitations note (Jan 22, 2026):** explicitly warns time horizon ≠ autonomous-run duration, and converting to delegation requires "how much time a human spends prompting AIs, waiting for generations, checking AI output… This process is nontrivial."
- **Claude Code / Codex note** ([Feb 13, 2026](https://metr.org/notes/2026-02-13-measuring-time-horizon-using-claude-code-and-codex/)): Opus 4.5 + Claude Code ≈ ReAct (beats it in only 50.7% of bootstraps); GPT-5 + Codex *under*performs Triframe (14.5%). Key framing: these tools "are mostly used in an interactive setting, where a human user often checks in on the agent's work" — fully autonomous runs surfaced failure modes (talking to a nonexistent user; over-anchoring on a plan).
- **Implication for a ~10 h autonomous case** (derived, not a METR quote): 10 h is at/above the best mid-2026 *50%* horizons and ~3–10x beyond *80%* horizons; since each +~2.3x reliability step (50→80%) costs ~5x in horizon and 99% is unfittable, unsupervised 10 h blocks imply coin-flip-or-worse reliability — METR's own framing says to size check-in cadence to the 80% (~1–3 h) horizon, not the 50% one.
- ⚠️ Unconfirmable: I found no METR publication giving a specific recommended oversight interval or a direct "max unattended runtime" measurement; the org-uplift note (Mar 19, 2026) exists but is anecdotal.

(Meta), [arXiv:2506.09985](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09985) + [Meta blog](https://ai.meta.com/blog/v-jepa-2-world-model-benchmarks/) (Jun 2025) | Pretrained on >1M hours of video + <62h robot video; zero-shot Franka pick-and-place at 65–80% success in unseen environments | Real evidence of video-pretrained world models doing manipulation planning — but MPC over learned latents is slow, nowhere near reactive catch rates |

| **UniSim** | Yang et al., [arXiv:2310.06114](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06114), [ICLR 2024 Outstanding Paper](https://blog.iclr.cc/2024/05/06/iclr-2024-outstanding-paper-awards/) | Policies trained purely in the learned simulator deploy zero-shot in the real world | Proof-of-concept that a learned sim can substitute for a physics engine — at enormous compute cost, and at visual-outcome (not force/contact) fidelity |

### A.2 The strongest case FOR learned models (the attempted refutation)

This is where your first-principles judgment takes real damage — not from Dreamer/Genie-class models, but from **residual/hybrid** work:

- **TossingBot** (Zeng et al., RSS 2019 / T-RO 2020 Best Paper, [arXiv:1903.11239](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.11239)) — *the closest comparable to drone-catch: ballistic throwing to a target.* Real-robot throw accuracy: **residual physics 84.7% vs analytic ballistics alone 61.3% vs pure learning 54.2%**. Drag on light objects and off-COM grasps make the analytic release velocity *systematically biased*. **Takeaway: in your exact task family, analytic-prior + learned residual beat analytics alone by 23 points.**
- **NeuroBEM** (Bauersfeld et al., RSS 2021, [arXiv:2106.08015](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.08015)) — *your exact vehicle class.* Blade-element analytic model + learned residual: **~50% force/torque RMSE reduction**; closed-loop tracking 0.8 m → <0.3 m. Ablation: hybrid beats both pure analytic AND pure learned (learned-only fails to generalize). **Takeaway: for quadrotors, first principles leave half the force error on the table.**
- **Neural-Fly** (O'Connell et al., Science Robotics May 2022, [DOI](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/scirobotics.abm6597)) — learned residual aerodynamics from **12 minutes** of flight data: tracking error in 12.1 m/s wind **8.7 cm vs 21.6 cm** nonlinear baseline (66% better). **Takeaway: the winning architecture is "analytic where it's right, learned where it's wrong."**
- **Contact specifically** — the part most relevant to your rigid-contact artifact:
  - **Bauza & Rodriguez** (ICRA 2017, [arXiv:1704.03033](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.03033)) + the "Million Ways to Be Pushed" dataset: real frictional contact is **stochastic and analytic models are biased on average**; a learned GP model beats the analytic pushing model after **<100 real samples**.
  - **ContactNets** (Pfrommer, Halm, Posa, CoRL 2020, [arXiv:2009.11193](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.11193)): structured learning (implicit signed distance + contact Jacobians) predicts real tossed-cube impacts/stiction from **60 seconds of data** where end-to-end nets fail.
  - **Parmar, Halm, Posa** (IROS 2021, [arXiv:2103.15406](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.15406)): stiff contact breaks *naive* deep learning — but the same paper flags that the compliant-contact settings sims use for numerical stability **don't reflect rigid hardware either**. Neither side is ground truth for contact.
  - **NeuralSim** (Heiden, Millard, **Coumans** et al., ICRA 2021, [arXiv:2011.04217](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.04217)): neural augmentation *inside* a differentiable rigid-body engine — co-authored by PyBullet's own creator, who argues analytic engines "can only predict systems for which they have been designed."

**The honest boundary of the refutation:** every quantitative win above is a learned residual **fit to real-world data**, correcting an analytic-model/reality gap. *No paper shows a learned model beating PyBullet at predicting PyBullet.* Inside a pure-sim project, the analytic sim is tautologically ground truth; a learned copy can only add error (plus rollout speed, the actual argument for learned models in pure-sim settings).

### A.4 Verdict

**Your judgment survives, but narrower than stated.** For a small classical-control prototyping project on known rigid-body dynamics in pure simulation, nothing in the literature recommends a Dreamer/Genie/JEPA-class learned world model — the field's own evidence (short trusted-rollout lengths, conservation-law violations, case-based generalization, 10⁴⁺-hour data costs, no ground-truth eval) supports "the sim IS the world model" *in-sim*. **Where it breaks:** the claim "known rigid-body dynamics" is false at exactly the two places your project physically lives — aerodynamics (NeuroBEM: 50% of quadrotor force error is unmodeled; TossingBot: drag bias costs 23 points of throw accuracy) and contact (real contact is stochastic, analytic models biased, and the soft-contact settings sims need for stability misrepresent rigid hardware — your rigid-contact artifact is a documented class of problem, and the literature's fix is *structured/residual learning on real data*, e.g. ContactNets, not more solver faith). The field's recommended architecture at the sim2real boundary is unambiguous: **analytic prior + learned residual**, which beat both parents in every head-to-head found. So: correct verdict for today's pure-PyBullet scope; the moment the project touches propwash, Re-dependent drag, or real hardware, the literature says add a learned residual — not a learned world model.

### B.1 METR time-horizon metric + trend

- **"Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks"** — Kwa, West et al., METR, [blog Mar 19 2025](https://metr.org/blog/2025-03-19-measuring-ai-ability-to-complete-long-tasks/) + [arXiv:2503.14499](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499) (v3 Feb 2026). Metric: the human-time length of tasks a model completes at 50% success. **Doubling ~every 7 months since 2019** ("may have accelerated in 2024"). Claude 3.7 Sonnet ≈ **1 hour** (TH1.1 re-estimate: 60.4 min [33–104]). Extrapolation: 1-month (167 work-hour) tasks between **mid-2028 and mid-2031**. *Takeaway: horizon growth is exponential and measured, not vibes.*
- **2025–2026 updates** ([metr.org/time-horizons](https://metr.org/time-horizons/), updated May 2026; [TH1.1, Jan 2026](https://metr.org/blog/2026-1-29-time-horizon-1-1/); [GPT-5 report, Aug 2025](https://metr.org/evaluations/gpt-5-report/)): post-2023 doubling re-estimated at **131 days**, post-2024 **89 days**. Frontier 50%-horizons: GPT-5 3h23m, Claude Opus 4.5 **4h53m**, Gemini 3.1 Pro 6h24m, Claude Opus 4.6 ~12h [5.3–60h] — with METR's own caveat that **measurements above 16h are unreliable** on the current suite. *Takeaway: mid-2026 frontier 50%-horizons are ~5–12h, doubling every ~3–4.5 months — with wide error bars METR itself flags.*

### B.2 Reliability falloff and the 50%→99% gap

- **80% horizons are 4–6× shorter than 50% horizons** (paper v1: "roughly 5×"; v3: "4–6×"), with the same doubling rate. Current 80%-horizons: ~25–90 min for most frontier models (e.g., GPT-5 ~38 min, Opus 4.5 ~49 min vs its 4h53m 50%-horizon). *Takeaway: each reliability step costs ~5× in horizon.*
- **99% horizons cannot be measured**: METR's [limitations note (Jan 22, 2026)](https://metr.org/notes/2026-01-22-time-horizon-limitations/) — "time horizons at 99%+ reliability levels cannot be fit at all without much larger and higher-quality benchmarks," and "a 50% time horizon of X hours does not mean we can delegate tasks under X hours." *Takeaway: reliability, not raw capability, is the binding constraint for delegation.*
- **Falloff shape/mechanism**: METR fits a logistic in log task length (R²≈0.80); **HCAST** ([arXiv:2503.17354](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.17354), Mar 2025): agents succeed 70–80% on <1h tasks, <20% on >4h tasks. **Sinha et al.** ([arXiv:2509.09677](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09677), Sep 2025, ICLR 2026): small per-step accuracy gains compound exponentially into task length; identifies **self-conditioning** — models get *more* error-prone with their own past mistakes in context. *Takeaway: failure at long horizons is compounding per-step error amplified by self-conditioning.*
- **Implication for a ~10h agent case** (derived from the above, not a METR quote): 10h sits at/above the best mid-2026 50%-horizons and 3–10× beyond 80%-horizons — an unsupervised 10h block implies coin-flip-or-worse completion odds; METR's framing (incl. the [Claude Code/Codex note, Feb 2026](https://metr.org/notes/2026-02-13-measuring-time-horizon-using-claude-code-and-codex/), which observes these tools are used interactively with human check-ins) points to sizing check-in cadence to the **80% horizon (~1–3h)**, not the 50% one.
